summary: Comments from Abhay Bhushan on the File Transfer Protocol in RFC 354. They include corrections to errors in the text, extra discussion, points to stress and additions to the protocol. He says he will fold them into the main document after enough experience.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo collects corrections and additions for the FTP specification in RFC 354. It clarifies server requirements, file-transfer behavior, mail commands, and how clients should prepare data connections.

subtitle: Clarifies requirements and adds commands and transfer details to the 1972 FTP specification.

tldr.problem: The FTP specification in RFC 354 needed corrections, clearer implementation requirements, and additional transfer and mail-handling details.
tldr.mechanism: This memo corrects text, clarifies default server requirements, defines mail commands and a reply code, and adds guidance for data connections and transfer modes.
tldr.outcome: The author intended to fold the comments into the main FTP protocol document after more experience. Unit metadata lists RFC 414 as an update.

today: RFC 385 is an update to RFC 354 and is itself updated by RFC 414, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Corrections and Required Defaults
sections.content:
The memo lists editorial corrections to RFC 354 and says its default FTP parameters should be treated as required for minimum server implementations. Those defaults include ASCII type, stream mode, file structure, and a core set of commands such as RETR, STOR, USER, PASS, SOCK, and BYE.

It also clarifies print-file types and explains trade-offs in stream mode, including uncertainty about using connection closure as end-of-file and CR-LF as an end-of-record without prior agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo corrects errors and makes some default server features minimum requirements. It also clarifies how file types and stream-mode endings should be understood.

sections.title: Data Connections and Transfer Rules
sections.content:
A user FTP process should listen on the data socket before sending a command that requires a transfer. A reply about the server's data socket may arrive after the connection request, so waiting for the reply before listening can cause problems.

The memo adds reply code 454 for failure to connect to the client's data socket. It also clarifies block-mode descriptor handling, says EOF is an implicit EOR, and recommends closing a data connection immediately after a transfer if it is to be closed.
sections.plainLanguage: The client should prepare its data connection before asking the server to transfer a file. The memo also clarifies how transfer errors and end markers are reported.

sections.title: Mail and Account Commands
sections.content:
The memo defines MLFL to send a file as mail to a user or designated site destination. It also defines MAIL for sending mail text over the Telnet connection, ending the message with a line containing only a period.

An ACCT command provides an account identifier for systems that need one in addition to a user name and password. The memo says FTP commands and type, mode, and structure symbols are case-insensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP gains separate commands for mailing a file, sending mail text, and supplying an account name. The memo also makes clear how these commands are written and terminated.

sections.title: Experimental Extensions
sections.content:
Sites may define experimental FTP commands. The memo says these commands should begin with the letter X; if they need new reply codes, those should be chosen in the range 900 through 999.

If an experimental command proves generally useful, the memo says it should be added to the standard FTP command set.
sections.plainLanguage: Sites can try FTP commands of their own using names that begin with X. A broadly useful command can later be considered for the shared command set.
